title: Clinical Clerkship, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
paragraphs: Clerkship in Shanghai, practice: a meeting from 7:45, then clerkship in the reading room (in OSCE style, I stated the findings and diagnosis one image at a time, and the attending answered); I went home at 19:00. The doctors sometimes stay overtime until past 22:00 and are busy. The basic system was three shifts, 365 days a year. I ate morning, noon and evening all at the hospital canteen, and at noon and in the evening a supervisor was present. The Radiology department of Ruijin Hospital means reading CT, MRI and radiographs, and IR, Rad-on, US and nuclear medicine are separate specialties, so it is quite subdivided, and it was mainly abdominal (pancreas). Dr. 缪, who is called the god of diagnostics, also presented me with two high-quality image collections of the pancreas and small intestine, as thick as SQUIRE'S FUNDAMENTALS OF RADIOLOGY, and I deepened my knowledge night after night. On holidays too I took part in Emergency Radiology (mainly MSK, KUB, chest radiograph) and studied thoroughly; there were days with 147 images in a day. In Japan, I think chest radiographs on holidays are on-call work, and I don't think they are even read on weekdays. That is different. An impressive case was an azygos lobe, a type of variant anatomy. At the meetings, neuro and body I could understand or knew, but MSK was tough, and unfortunately I found holes in my knowledge, which became a future task, and I worked to improve. As a result, thanks to that effort and to my advance preparation, I received Grade 95/100 on Ruijin Hospital's own evaluation form. I felt I had obtained a good result, and it was also evaluated objectively.

Clerkship at TCM: a two-week clerkship, and here I was in the same cohort as an exchange student (fourth year) from New York, URMC. It was reassuring to have my first fellow cohort member since coming here. There was a table round from 8:00, and after that we went around the TCM oncology ward and did rounds on patients. Western technology had also been introduced, and it functioned as a palliative care unit and as family medicine and also ran clinical trials. In TCM I was also shown many herbs in clinical trials. I was also allowed to do the physical, and in particular I was taught the basic examinations of the right radial artery (I learned the bracelet-type method too) and looking at the tongue. In the afternoon I went to the TCM tuina department and was allowed to actually give massage to patients. The purpose is to relax the muscles. The doctors were stout with thick arms, and it was impressive that even when force was applied they were supple rather than strained. Being able to take part in the clinical setting in this way was educational for me. Besides that, they also followed up joint range of motion and corrected the trunk using instruments. I was also allowed to take part in the clerkships in the outpatient clinic, TCM pharmacy, moxibustion and acupuncture. Acupuncture differs from that in the West (it seems to be covered by insurance in the United States) and that in Japan in that the needles are inserted deeply and it is quite painful. TCM theory differs from WM, but within a history of 5000 years, a fusion of West and China has occurred in the last half century. In this department I learned medical interviewing, the basics of examination, and the 5000-year history and concepts of Chinese medicine, which gave me more breadth as a future physician.

After that I visited neurosurgery for one week. After rounds, from the first day, I was allowed to assist in the surgical field in both Jannetta operations. In the second case, a better skill than in the first was required. For example, in the first case I only watched the cover being put on the Leica, but in the next I did it myself. I always approached it with this thinking: the first time, watch and steal the technique; the second time, do it myself. Unlike at Nagoya University, the surgical attire is not a student uniform but always the same clothes as the doctors, and in the same color, so there were times when I did work that nurses do at Nagoya University, and I felt the responsibility of taking part in clinical practice. From the third Jannetta case, I was also allowed to do skin suturing. Being allowed to suture in a foreign land was a truly good experience and at the same time gave me confidence. Besides entering surgery, I took part in the specialist outpatient clinic run by my supervising doctor. In his specialty, my supervisor has China's number one surgical technique and success rate, and patients came to Ruijin Hospital from all over the country (from Uyghur in the northwest to Wuhan in the southeast). Many said they had come because the operation they had received at another hospital had not cured them. Besides taking histories, I read CTs from other hospitals that they brought (I could use the knowledge I had cultivated in neuroradiology in another department too, which led to confidence). Neurosurgery in particular seems to have exchanges with foreign countries, and my supervisor is also the president of an Asian society meeting in Shanghai, and 20 people from Japan are reportedly attending this meeting. I sincerely think that by my doing a clerkship in neurosurgery, exchange has broadened and I have contributed to the international reputation of the Nagoya University School of Medicine.

Clerkship in respiratory diseases: a two-week clerkship, and of the clerkships in Shanghai, this department was the first and last where I had the opportunity to interact with local students and do the clerkship together. The clerkship began with a table round at 7:30, then rounds, and after that, as students' work, we did blood pressure measurement and EKGs and so on. A respiratory medicine doctor asked me to translate an article of a Japanese respiratory society journal, and I was able to help with it. There was also a time when I was asked what to do because it is not in PubMed, which was quite a problem. Japanese-language papers are of course not in PubMed (there may be some). It was a disease with only 35 cases reported in the world and 3 in Japan at the time. The treatment policy was expected to be extremely difficult, and it was a tragedy for the patient too. Besides that, from the third year they do combined lectures, with classroom study and case discussion in the morning and hospital clerkship from noon, which is apparently special even in Shanghai. I was surprised. They took histories and then presented on the cases.

Clerkship at the Department of Hypertension and Shanghai Institution of Hypertension: table round from 8:00, then rounds, panel discussion from 12:00, and then clerkship in the laboratory as it was. I also took part in the outpatient clinic, but here too they were collecting research data, and my impression was of energetic research. Hypertension is not an independent department at our Nagoya University Hospital, so it was very educational. I saw diseases corresponding to nephrology, endocrinology, neurology, cardiology, respiratory medicine, obstetrics and gynecology, ophthalmology and so on. Also there are five or fewer institutes of hypertension in China, so it is a very valuable experience. In Japan ABI is one of the well-known indicators of hypertension, but there are many other parameters too, and I am beginning by understanding the test method of each and what the outcome means. As is well known, in Asia, because the diet differs from the West, applying Western reference values and target values as they are can be a reference but does not make much sense. For example, salt intake is overwhelmingly highest in East Asia. If it is the same Asia, I thought what I learned here could be put to use, and I work at my daily studies.

Life: it is within a 10-minute walk from the dormitory to Ruijin Hospital. As for extracurricular activities, I have not been able to do them at present because the clerkship was very busy and tough. In the dormitory there is one Japanese first-year student of Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, and this is the first time I have met a Japanese person here. I plan to deepen our friendship. When I casually asked about their background, they have lived in Osaka, San Diego and Shanghai and are very experienced despite being in their early twenties. They helped me when I was in trouble.

(Brief summary) At Ruijin Hospital alone, I did clerkships in five clinical departments. I heard that Japanese students basically come for one month and that three months is a first. It is the foremost hospital in Shanghai, and a famous doctor takes the histories of 100 patients a day, with nearly 3 million interviews a year. When I actually took part, I was simply astonished by the patients pressing in one after another in rapid succession, the long lines at the elevators and the 22-story clinic. In addition there is a 1700-bed ward, and I am speechless.
